A generative language model is a decoder (

) pretrained to predict the next token. Generating text is nothing more than repeating this prediction: the model computes a probability distribution over its vocabulary, one token is chosen, it is appended to the input, and the model predicts again. How the token is chosen matters a great deal. The same model can be deterministic or creative, repetitive or varied, depending on its decoding strategy. This section follows the loop with a small open model, SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, whose 135 million parameters run on a laptop processor at about 26 tokens per second.

The model does not look up a fact. It has learned which continuations are likely after such a sentence, and many continuations are: “the city of ...”, a city name, “located in ...”. The correct answer, Bern, has slightly less probability than Geneva, which is wrong. A larger model trained on more data concentrates more probability on Bern, but the principle stays the same: the output is drawn from a distribution over plausible text.

Such fluent but false statements are called

. They are not a malfunction but a consequence of the mechanism: the model produces likely text, and likely text is not always true. Larger models hallucinate less on common facts, but they still do so on rare facts, recent events, and questions outside their training data. This is the main reason why retrieval-augmented generation (
) gives the model the relevant documents and asks it to answer from them.

A model pretrained on next-token prediction continues text; it does not follow instructions. Asked a question, it may continue with more questions. Turning it into an assistant takes two further training stages.
, a supervised fine-tuning on pairs of instructions and good responses, teaches the model to answer.
then teaches it which of several possible answers people prefer. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (
) trains a reward model on human rankings of answers and tunes the language model to maximize the reward;
(DPO) reaches a similar result with a simple classification loss on pairs of preferred and rejected answers, without a separate reward model.

The Context Window and the KV Cache

children.label: The Context Window and the KV Cache

children.value: is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to: 8,192 for SmolLM2, and between 128,000 and a million tokens for current large models. Everything the model should consider must fit into it: the system instructions, the conversation so far, retrieved documents, and the answer being generated. Longer contexts are not used uniformly. Liu and colleagues showed that models use information at the beginning and the end of a long context much better than information in the middle, a reason why
cares about which passages enter the prompt and where.
Generation runs in two phases. In the
phase, the model processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass, like an encoder. In the
phase, it generates one token at a time. To avoid recomputing the keys and values of all previous tokens at every step, it stores them in the
and only computes the new token’s query, key, and value. The cache grows with every token, and for long contexts it, not the model weights, fills the memory of the graphics processor:

computes 1 GiB per 8,192 tokens for an 8B model with grouped-query attention. Serving systems such as vLLM therefore manage the cache in fixed-size blocks, like the pages of an operating system, to fit more requests into memory.
Large language models can learn a task from the prompt alone, without any change to their weights. A
prompt adds a few solved examples, from which the model infers the pattern; GPT-3 showed in 2020 that this ability emerges with scale.

prompting asks the model to write intermediate reasoning steps before the answer, which improves its accuracy on problems that need several steps, such as arithmetic word problems. Recent reasoning models are trained to produce such steps on their own.

Prompting has costs. A prompt adds tokens, and every token costs time and money. The output can vary from run to run, and small changes to the wording can change the result. Many applications need machine-readable output instead of prose, for example a JSON object with a label and extracted fields. A prompt can ask for JSON and describe its fields, but a model may still produce invalid JSON or invent fields.

guarantees the format: at each step, it sets the probability of every token to zero that would violate a grammar or a JSON schema, so the model can only generate valid output. Most serving systems and model APIs offer such structured output modes.
Confidence values in generated text are not probabilities

A model asked to output a confidence for each label writes numbers that look like probabilities but are just more generated text. In an earlier version of this material, a model classified the opening of Arthur Conan Doyle’s novel
